review_text_raw: The weakest of the Simulacra Trilogy by far (even Pipe Dreams felt more comprehensive as a horror experience). It feels like the budget for this game was severely cut. There are many features missing in this game that were present in the previous, the horror elements are few and far between, and obvious bugs still remaining in the game (as of Sept 2026). The audio mixing clearly has issues with some dialogue being so quiet I have to bump up my volume a considerable amount, only later to have my eardrums blasted by one of Paul's vlog videos. The characters have almost no interesting traits and the writing feels flat. Your responses barely seem to matter for most of the game... what happened to being able to lie convincingly to people over texts? Having your character spill the beans about who they are under the slightest bit of pressure takes all the fun out of choosing unique dialogue. Speaking of the dialogue, it is SLOW with no option for increasing text speed- this made getting all achievements an absolute slog. Overall, I expected more from the final entry in this series. I put off playing this game for a long time because the reviews were very mixed, and this sadly confirmed my expectations of the quality of this game. Maybe pick this up if you still want more Simulacra after playing the first two games, but don't expect the same level of quality.

This review includes spoilers: 

I really loved Simulacra 1 and 2 and I replayed them right before the 3. within the last couple of days.
And I've gotta say, I really don't like the main simulacrum in this game. It is way less scary to have a literal monster as the main villain instead of something that possesses humans in my opinion. 

There is also a lack of social commentary, because of that. I've always interpreted the first and second game as social commentaries on smartphone / media addiction. The first one dealt with the negative side of dating apps, the second game dealt with being an influencer and addicted to being famous. This entry does none of that. It's not a social commentary on creepypasta / digital horror, like I thought it would be. 

I also think there are weirdly enough several downgrades in comparison to the 2nd game, which was really weird to me. The UI feels unintuitive, none of your decisions really seemed to influence the people around you, there is no character growth. 

The puzzles feel illogical. Maybe I was too dumb for them, but I don't think the game gives you enough hints to figure out what exactly you are supposed to do at certain points. The hint system was also weirdly useless in this game. 

But I really did like the atlas features (except for the tracing route mode) and the "live" segments.

I'm really sorry to leave this review, I still love this franchise as a whole, but this one just wasn't for me.

review_text_raw:
[Review after completing 100% of current content]

This is a game marred by a clear disconnect between what narrative the audience expects, and what the creators want to tell. The original horror executed its concept well with its meta elements that weren't present in this new experience turned "deep narrative" about the gentrification of a small community. Remembering its roots, I could count the amount of horror moments in Simulacra 3 with a single-fingered hand. Rook-your character-crumpling like paper could certainly be seen as horror, with his flimsy attempts to push consequences on those around him.

The puzzles felt immature and insulting at best, while tedious and hintless at worst. These ranging from reading two posts on their limited feed to tracing paths that were directly communicated; a confusing case with reviews mentioning the need to "pay close attention." Surprises in narrative were few and far between, boiling down to the Simulacra coming in like a disappointing WWE wrestler that you wished wasn't part of the new arc. Pushed by "Big Horror" in an otherwise new space.

The mixed art form in the single truly interactive camera segment was exciting, teasing more diverse gameplay segments. Pity. That was all. Truly, a pity, with the acting of Ruby and Paul being a joy to see, reminding me of passionate youth theatre. It fell quickly back to its trudging phone interface that felt like a nightmare for subsequent playthroughs. Getting all the ending cards felt like a punishment rather than a reward.

Please purge your mind of previous entries if you're going to give this a go, and be ready to spend more time reading meaningless social feeds to fish for info used in two more obtuse puzzles. Keep in mind, this remains the most expensive entry in the series.

Do you just expect people play it once? You have multiple endings, you go out of your way to describe the ending, and you even have a dedicated button for endings on the main menu. Why should it be so painful to go back through everything I just read and discovered at the same speed?

A step-down from the last two installments. Compared to Simulacra 1 and 2, this is... pretty bad. Meh-ish. Semi-spoilers down below!
I don't mind the game's antagonist. If you've read other reviews where it says it's a ghost, the answer to that is a yes and a no. It's still a simulacra, but it takes a form of a ghost that's popular in the town's folklore and media.
That aside, the devs had made this installment rather boring and plain. You'd expect something more complex and interesting compared to the last game, but it's just... a huge down-grade from that. And I didn't even hate the second one! It was good!
BUUUT! Credit where credit's due: certain sequences are rather tense (like the entirety of Paul's house thing), and it works really well. I quite like the Atlas tracking functions, too. Ruby's actress is good, and Paul's actor is good at voice acting, so it isn't ENTIRELY bad.
Still, if you, like me, wanted to just play every installments of this franchise, just wait for the discount and get the bundle edition, since if you have the last two games, it will save you at least 30 cents if you just bought it seperately.
Overall, the experiance feels like the very first game minus the good with itty bitty of the new. Play at your own risk.

Honestly, this game is absolutely nothing like Simulacra 1 & 2. There's not that many routes to take, there's no comedic relief, hardly any relationships between anyone, and etc. It doesn't necessarily feel like a real Simulacra type thing either even though it technically is. So yeah, I wouldn't recommend this for anyone who likes Simulacra 1 and 2. BUT, if you prefer Sara is Missing, then this is a more intense version of that game. This one doesn't have the same type of replayable feeling as 1 and 2, even though it is replayable. Just didn't have a lot of enthusiasm and was way too serious for my tastes. It was definitely a let-down compared to the previous versions.

review_text_raw: I really enjoyed simulacra 1, pipe dreams, and 2 was honestly really cool. But this isn't it. My biggest peeve with this franchise is that it NEVER continues any kind of overarching story, theres never a bigger picture, they always seem to act like there will be but it never happens. The end of Sim 2 made me think this game would be on a large grand scale, a climax involving the simulacras, but it just fell short and the entire game was predictable. I got the best ending on my first try and it was extremely easy to keep everybody alive, and the other games were difficult to get the best ending. I liked that about the other games, it added mystery and replayability. But this game I got the best outcome on my first attempt without any prior knowledge about anything and that is very disappointing to me and makes me have no desire to really go through it all again. The second game was great because it took me at least a few attempts to get the best ending and I remember being genuinely stumped as to what was going on or whodunnit, but I never felt that with this game. Nothing was a mystery to me, I could see everything coming from a mile away. And there was nothing scary either, just a couple cheap scenes with the phones background and that's it. The first two games the background changes throughout and it makes you feel unsettled and its cool to see, but this game just felt... lazy. It feels like the bare minimum and I was really hoping it would be better, but the reason I didn't want to play this game stood true. I feel like i wasted my time with it, but I do hope if they make another game in this franchise, it's better. I really would like to enjoy the series again, but right now, its just repetitive, nothing new happens, its just the exact same situation in each game and nothing in this world they are creating changes. It doesn't feel like the simulacrums are an actual problem, just a minor inconvenience once in a blue moon. I hope the devs read reviews because I saw a lot of people with similar opinions to mine and I would love to see a sim 4 where something new finally develops in this world their building instead of just same shit different day.

review_text_raw:
This one takes itself far too seriously while having the weakest story of the three. The novelty and tightness of part 1 are absent which wouldn't be so bad, but gone also are the goofy charms of the cast and various interactions of part 2. Simulacra 3 is stripped down to be a relatively joyless and linear experience.

Thematically, and there is really no nice way to say this, but this game is like a JHorror movie trying to pass its setting off as being in small town America despite it having the least (as in none) American cast and a very clearly JHorror inspired villain. The story would have been much better served if it were just set in Malaysia and based on some kind of Malaysian folklore. It's hard to take the American small town setting seriously when Old MacDonald's farm has the kind of international phone number you might expect in Hong Kong and literally every single character has a different accent from various parts of the globe. Stick to the bundle that has the first two.

review_text_raw:
I really wanted to like this game, I really did. 

I loved the previous Simulacra titles, I loved what they did, how they tackled topics of online life from a very different perspective, I loved the variety of characters and the decisions you got to make about them. And mostly, it was just incredibly fun stalking through someone's phone, through social media, seeing other people react to things in realtime, it wasn't 100% convincing, but it made all of it feel a lot more real. And I loved the feeling of danger when getting in contact and confronting the Entities yourself, it was engaging and scary and amazing storytelling.

All of this is gone here.

Let's start with the concept, the previous titles revolved around some current digital topics, online dating, influencers or predatory games. This game mostly drops the digital. It's a ghost story in a town followed through a Maps-App. There's so many topics that could've fit amazingly - NFT's, VR, AR, even Covid and being forced to be home (which admittedly does come up but in a shallow and meaningless way). But we got a Maps-App and a town-mystery, with themes of power, government, community and the interaction of urban myth and history. This too could potentially have been something interesting, but no. 

The story is maybe the most okay part about this game, the town myth is set up nicely, but quite basic, there are some interesting twists and misdirections, and I loved the part about how all of the events started [spoiler]Amy is just a really cool and interesting character[/spoiler]. But many parts absolutely do not work. Some are really forced like [spoiler]when we have to decieve the poor receptionist and cost her her job because Ruby didn't tell us what she was going to do[/spoiler] and the story also doesn't get nearly enough breathing room to work. Especially because you have to work with different characters and convince them of things, yet you've barely interacted before. It doesn't feel like you're participating in a story but playing a bad puzzle game.

The characters are okay-ish, the one you're interacting most with is Ruby and she's written as though you're meant to form a connection, but I just didn't, I didn't feel that much for her or care that much about her, so the emotional core that's built around her just doesn't work. There are some other characters I liked a lot more like [spoiler]Persephone / Damien and Carin[/spoiler] they're fun interacting with and they have personality, but they're also barely there. And even them are just lame compared to the fun interactions with Murillo or unhinged rants of Aria in Simulacra 2, who just felt like real people, with their own desires, hopes, dreams and delusions.

The horror / scary parts are just completely gone. It's so sad, the previous parts could pull you in so much, through the phone glitching or asking invasive or interesting questions, and create a real sense of dread, but here you don't ever feel in danger, because you never are. How would you feel in danger if the Beldam works by [spoiler]ppl seeing graffiti that wasn't there before, or encountering that eye symbol[/spoiler] which are mostly just tied to the real world. Nothing is i.e. indicating you've forgotten time, like that could've been a great point of tension, like a glitch followed by Ruby calling you and asking where you've been the last days. But nothing interesting or scary happens to you. I'd say the most tense sequence was [spoiler]getting Ruby out of Paul's House[/spoiler] but even there you weren't under time pressure, you didn't have to account for it moving, it wasn't challenging at all. Like [spoiler]electronics drew in the Beldam, her phone could've slowly drawn the Beldam towards her unless you activated something else[/spoiler]. And the Beldam itself isn't scary either. The previous Simulacra were always abstract, unfathomable, which made them scary and interesting, but giving the Beldam a bad CGI form didn't do the "horror" any favors. 

The mechanics in the game and the puzzles were also just lame. Most of it is very bland and unoriginal and the Atlas app (maps) is probably the worst of all. It's such a hacked together mess that doesn't make sense as a piece of software, especially the tracking function, and the hints in that function just make everything a lot worse. Like [spoiler]Thomas favorite place gives you the hint with the coffee order. At first I thought, hey there's this dude rating the Beldam locations, maybe I have to bring that in order? Nope. It says something about chronology, maybe I have to sort the ratings by the date posted? Nope. Oh it says something about a specific order in the description, I saw the post like that (@leftOnRead) might it be the places from which this account posted in order? Nope. What I didn't know was that I wasn't far enough and didn't have the grind, park and bus stop on the map yet.[/spoiler] I wasted so much time because of the hint system trying to solve something I couldn't yet.

The previous titles made you feel smart for figuring stuff out, piecing it together, hacking into things, especially because you had a "real phone", from another person, where you just had to circumvent things, but this game does the horrible mistake of dropping all pretenses. It's not a phone from a person missing, it's a puzzle box by a nerd who doesn't wanna give you straightforward information. There's nothing personal in there. NOTHING. No photos, no chats, everything is locked in his fun juiced up Atlas version. You don't try to outsmart technology to gather hidden intel, you have to get around the tedious roadblocks put in place by the informant - why, exactly? At first it's framed like he only had time to send the phone, but then WHY did he make the effort of hiding everything in these tedious puzzles? Especially when he wanted the information to get out and Ruby able to act. The "social media" (everything you get is the social page on the Atlas app) is sadly also incredibly sparse. There's a few posts you can go through, but where in S2 these mattered and you got to know more about the characters and some characters you would later interact with, here in S3 they barely matter at all. They're not engaging to read through, nor interesting discusssions, they're just lame filler. All of the fun of peeking into someone else's life is gone.
